It's pretty easy to install, but there are a couple things you can fuck up.

Your first step is to burn the install .iso file to a dvd disc or a usb thumbdrive. I recommend a program called Win32 Disk Imager https://sourceforge.net/projects/win32diskimager/ It's very simple to use. Pick the file to burn, choose and doublecheck the drive to burn it to, then click write.

Your next step is to boot your PC from the thumbdrive. You may have to use your UEFI boot menu to do so, and to access that you may need to close windows in a special way because of secureboot. See this link https://www.howtogeek.com/175641/how-to-boot-and-install-linux-on-a-uefi-pc-with-secure-boot/

Once Linux has loaded from the thumbdrive you will be give the option to test it from the drive or install it immediately. If you choose to test it you can still install it from there.

Once you're ready to install you need to give it a partition to install to, which means using a spare drive, overwriting your windows drive (AND ALL THE DATA ON IT), or shrinking the windows partition on your windows drive and make a second partition on that drive for Linux.

Since one of those options includes deleting everything on your windows drive you want to make sure to not rush through and doublecheck everything before committing.

Linux describes drives as SDA, SDB, SDC... etc. and follows that with a number for the partition. When looking at the available partitions your windows partition will most likely be named SDA 2. SDA 1 would be the recovery partition for windows.

The installer should make everything pretty simple, but if you're unsure what's what use that. Also check drive sizes to make sure they look right.

Once you've decided where to install Linux, hit install. It will start installing and telling you things about how awesome Linux is. It will ask for an internet connection if you use wifi. It will ask if you want to install proprietary drivers/software. Unless you want to go full "I'm a strong black nerd that don't need no proprietary software man" I highly recommend installing them.

Once the install finishes, or maybe during, it will have you set up a username and password. You will need to make sure you remember your password, because Linux will ask you for it a lot more often than Windows did.

The very first things to do are check for and install updates. There are two ways to do this. One is to use Mint's built in graphical update utility. Basically you fire it up, put in your password, and let it do its thing. If it asks whether it can use repositories say yes.

The other way, which you WILL want to know, is to use the command line. In Mint you can access the command line by clicking a little icon in the bottom left of the screen for it, finding the application called Terminal in the "start" menu, or if stuff's gone really fucky you can use ctrl alt F1. After you have the terminal (CLI) open you would type in the command

sudo apt-get update

put in your password when prompted, and let it run to find all the stuff that needs updating. Then type in 

sudo apt-get upgrade

to install everything it found. Once you've done that try exploring Mint's introduction screen it opens on boot.

A few more CLI commands that you'll find very useful:

sudo shutdown now -r

What this does is tell the computer to shutdown now and restart (that's the -r, leave it off to just shutdown). With Linux you don't shit have updating after you shut down or when you boot like with Windows, so forcing a shutdown isn't needed too often, but if you need to, that's how.

xkill

This will turn your mouse cursor into an X symbol, and the next program you click will be forceably closed. Very handy if a program is misbehaving for some reason.

tab

When typing in directories and file names, you can type in the first part of the name then use the tab key to cycle through all the directories or files that match it. This makes navigating the folder structure and working with files from the CLI much easier and less frustrating than in Windows. (Although newer Windows has added in some tab completion too!)

One thing to note is that ctrl-a ctrl-c and ctrl-v do NOT do the standard copy/paste stuff in a terminal. highlight with the mouse and use the right click context menu for that stuff. You can also find some helpful stuff here https://community.linuxmint.com/tutorial/view/244 and here http://www.linuxandubuntu.com/home/10-basic-linux-commands-that-every-linux-newbies-should-remember

If you ever need to do advanced troubleshooting, Google is your friend, but the arch-wiki is your new god https://wiki.archlinux.org/ It's for a different distro of Linux than Mint, so it's not 100% compatible, but it's got all the information ever and is super helpful.
